entry.summary: Zod v4 is faster than v3. But almost nobody knows why. It's not just a cleaner codebase or smaller bundle — Zod v4 has a JIT-like code generator that builds specialized validation functions at runtime using new Function(). entry.title: Stop decompressing entire archives to get one file — introducing ARCX
entry.summary:
Most archive formats make a simple task unnecessarily expensive: you need one file, so you download and decompress everything. I built ARCX, a compressed archive format designed to fix that. ARCX combines cross-file compression (like tar+zstd) with indexed random access (like zip), so you can retrieve a single file from a large archive in milliseconds without decompressing the rest. GitHub: https://github.com/getarcx/arcx Install: cargo install arcx
Across 5 real-world datasets: ~7ms to retrieve a file from a ~200MB archive up to 200x less data read vs tar+zstd compression within ~3% of tar+zstd Example:
Dataset ARCX Bytes Read TAR+ZSTD Bytes Read Reduction
Python ML 326 KB 63.1 MB 198x less
Build Artifacts 714 KB 140.4 MB 202x less
Modern systems don't need entire archives. They need one file, immediately. This shows up in: CI/CD pipelines (artifacts) cloud storage (partial retrieval) large codebases package registries ARCX reduces archive access to a manifest lookup, one block read, and one block decompress. ARCX uses: block-based compression a binary manifest index direct offset reads Instead of scanning or decompressing the full archive: Look up the file in the index Seek to the relevant block Decompress only that block
Format Compression Selective Access
ZIP weaker fast
tar+zstd strong slow
ARCX strong fast
ARCX is not designed for streaming (like tar). The archive must be complete before reading because the manifest is written at the end. Remote/S3 range-read workflows not fully benchmarked yet Metadata/index overhead still being optimized for very large file counts Full extraction benchmarks in Rust are still in progress Still early -- feedback welcome.
